name: Woozle effect
statement: Repeated citation turns a weak or absent finding into an accepted fact, because each new citation reads as fresh support rather than a repetition of the same source.
meaning: The claim is about a literature rather than a person. A finding is stated once, tentatively or not at all, and later papers cite it. Later papers cite those. To an author arriving in the field, the pile of references looks like a body of evidence, so the claim is repeated again and the pile grows. Nielsen reports that Gelles called this process evidence by citation. Two things make it hard to see from inside. No single step is dishonest, since every author cites a real document that really says what is attributed to it. And the pile grows faster than the data, because a review paper can be cited for a claim without containing any measurement of it. What ends up carrying the belief is the shape of the citation graph, not the strength of the studies at its root.

origin.where: Journal of Marriage and the Family
origin.note: Gelles reviewed a decade of family violence research and described claims that had gained standing through repeated citation rather than through new data. His paper was not obtained, and that account comes from Nielsen's 2014 article. Nielsen says Gelles popularised the concept and credits the term woozle effect to Beverly Houghton, whose paper 'Review of research on women and abuse' was given at the American Society of Criminology national conference in Philadelphia in November 1979. The woozle is from chapter three of Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh, in which Pooh and Piglet circle a spinney of larch trees after paw marks that multiply as they walk. Christopher Robin, watching from an oak tree, counts off the circuits they made, and Pooh then fits his own paw into one of the tracks.

evidence: The measured case is Steven Greenberg's 2009 citation network. He took the claim that beta amyloid is produced by and injures muscle in sporadic inclusion body myositis, collected every English language PubMed paper carrying a statement about it, and recorded which paper cited which for that statement. The network held 242 papers and 675 citations, of which 636 were supportive, 18 neutral and 21 critical. Counting chains rather than single links, 220,553 citation paths supported the claim against 28 that weakened it. Between 1996 and 2007 supportive citations grew sevenfold and supportive paths 777-fold. Six primary data papers held results that weakened or refuted the claim and were barely cited. Three of them, from independent laboratories, covered 35 patients: 28 had no affected muscle fibres and the other seven had five or fewer, in sections that hold thousands. Seventeen animal and cell culture papers made 32 citations to primary data, 31 of them to the four supportive papers and one to the six critical ones. One review paper carried 63% of all citation paths and four reviews by a single research group carried 95%. Greenberg also traced invention. One subclaim about timing appeared in 27 papers on 37 citations, nine of which pointed at papers saying nothing about timing. Seven papers made 17 citations to 12 conference abstracts dressed as peer reviewed papers. Rebuilding the network with the bias against critical content removed gave authority status to five of the six neglected papers. Vedrana Pavlovic and colleagues measured citation accuracy directly, asking the authors of cited papers to check. Across 2,526 citations to 14 heavily cited papers, and a verification set of 4,912 citations to 13 more, at least one inaccurate citation appeared in 11.1% and 15.0% of citing articles. Taking both sets together, the commonest fault at 38.4% was citing a finding the source did not contain. Chains in which an error was copied from an earlier citing paper carried 24% of the inaccurate citations in the first set and 19.3% in the second. Tzu-Kun Hsiao and Jodi Schneider looked at what happens after a paper is withdrawn: of 13,252 citation contexts written after a retraction, 722, or 5.4%, mentioned the retraction.

replication.headline: Greenberg's network design has since been run on six other biomedical questions, and four of the six showed citation bias.
replication.detail: Miriam Urlings and colleagues built citation networks for six biomedical research questions, mapped every citation that could have been made against those actually made, and modelled what predicted a citation. Four of the six networks showed evidence of citation bias. Self-citation, the authority of the author and journal impact factor raised the chance of being cited in all six. The surrounding literature is much larger. Bram Duyx and colleagues reviewed 47 publications carrying 52 studies of citation bias, and pooled the 21 with enough data to give a citation rate ratio for statistical significance. Articles with statistically significant results were cited 1.6 times as often as articles without, 95% CI 1.3 to 1.8. Across eight studies, articles whose authors concluded they had found support for their hypothesis were cited 2.7 times as often, CI 2.0 to 3.7. Heterogeneity was high and its source was not identified, and of the 52 studies 29 found a clear effect of outcome on citation, 11 found none and 12 were mixed. The authors report that almost all pointed the same way. Greenberg's fuller account has carried over unevenly. Janina Sarol, Jodi Schneider and Halil Kilicoglu tried to rebuild his coding automatically on the same network. They recovered amplification, picking out all four of the review papers that carry 95% of the citation paths. Their tools reached his conclusion on citation bias while classifying the primary data papers badly, scoring below 0.5 F1 and finding no critical ones at all by the route that used no language model. On invention both approaches did poorly, the best prompt for citation diversion returning two true positives among 200 predictions.

study.cite: Urlings, M. J. E., Duyx, B., Swaen, G. M. H., Bouter, L. M., & Zeegers, M. P. (2021). Citation bias and other determinants of citation in biomedical research: findings from six citation networks. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 132, 71-78.

limits: Greenberg studied one claim in one specialty, and one colleague validated his text and citation extraction for 17% of the papers. His analysis shows how the claim acquired authority. It does not test whether the claim is true, and he does not say it is false. Urlings and colleagues is open access under a CC BY licence, and none of the copies listed as open could be opened here: the publisher's PDF at jclinepi.com, the same article at ScienceDirect and the file at the VU Research Portal each returned a Cloudflare bot challenge on 21 September 2026, which is not a paywall and may not stop the next reader. The four-of-six figure is read from the abstract at Maastricht University's repository and at PubMed, and that abstract does not name the six research questions. Gelles's 1980 review was not obtained either. Its DOI resolves to JSTOR, which returned a bot challenge on the same date, and OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Internet Archive Scholar list no open copy, so the account of his argument and of Houghton's 1979 coinage comes from Nielsen. The most quoted single case is a five sentence 1980 letter to the New England Journal of Medicine reporting that addiction was rare among hospital inpatients given narcotics, counted by Leung and colleagues in 2017. OpenAlex lists both the letter and that 2017 correspondence as free at the publisher, and nejm.org returned a bot challenge for both on 21 September 2026, so neither was read here. Hao, Davis and Schatman give the result as 608 citations through 2017, 439 of them treating the letter as substantive evidence, and that is the route by which those two numbers reach this page. They have not been held against Leung. No experiment was located in which readers were shown a claim backed by many citations or by few and their belief in it measured, which is the form a psychological test of the effect would take. The nearest found is Jean-Francois Rouet and colleagues, who manipulated the citation counts attached to references and measured which ones students chose. In their third experiment the less relevant references were three times more likely to be selected when they carried a high number. Searches on 21 September 2026 covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar and Google via web search.
misreadings: The spinach story is the example most often reached for, and the standard telling of it is itself a woozle. Rekdal traced the chain. Arnold Bender said in a 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College that the fame of spinach may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point, and repeated the phrase in a book and an article three years later. By a 1977 letter to The Spectator it had hardened to 'appears to have been based on'. Terence Hamblin then printed it as fact in the BMJ of 19 to 26 December 1981, giving no reference for it, though his article carries a list of sources for its other stories. He put the original overestimate in the 1890s and the German re-analysis that corrected it in the 1930s. Bender's own textbook for medical students, written with D A Bender, fixed the error in 1982 to a specific year, 1870, two decades earlier than the date Hamblin had given. Mike Sutton asked Hamblin where he had read it; Hamblin could not remember and thought it might have been Reader's Digest. Rekdal reports no evidence that any decimal point error occurred, and gives Sutton's alternatives: contamination during analysis, and confusion between fresh and dried spinach. Hamblin acknowledged the mistake publicly before his death in February 2012. Telling the spinach anecdote as a documented case of citation drift commits the error it is offered to illustrate. A second misreading treats Greenberg as having disproved the amyloid claim. He argues the opposite of certainty: with the citation bias removed, belief in the claim's truth and its falseness would be balanced. The figure that only about 20% of citers have read what they cite is also weaker than it sounds. Simkin and Roychowdhury inferred it from the way misprints repeat across reference lists, so it is the output of a stochastic model rather than a count of readers. Pavlovic and colleagues' 11% and 15% are counts. And the Pooh story is about self-deception. The extra tracks belong to Pooh and Piglet, laid down as they circle the spinney, which makes it a picture of self-citation rather than of borrowing from strangers.
